source_text: Necesse est, quatenus hoc putas arbitrio tuo licuisse, ut aut impossibilem aut inconvenientem deo existimaveris nativitatem. Sed deo nihil impossibile nisi quod non vult. An ergo voluerit nasci (quia si voluit, et potuit et natus est) consideremus. Ad compendium decurro. Si enim nasci se deus noluisset, quacunque de causa. nec hominem se videri praestitisset. Nam quis hominem videns eum negaret natum? Ita quod noluisset esse, nec videri omnino voluisset. Omnis rei displicentis etiam opinio reprobatur, quia nihil interest utrum sit quid an non sit, si cum non sit esse praesumitur. Plane interest ut falsum non patiatur quod vere non est. Sed satis erat illi, inquis, conscientia sua. Viderint homines si natum putabant, quia hominem videbant. Quanto ergo dignius quantoque constantius humanam sustinuisset existimationem vere natus, eandem existimationem etiam non natus subiturus cum iniuria conscientiae suae quam tu ad fiduciam reputas, ut non natus adversus conscientiam suam natum se existimari sustineret? Quid tanti fuit edoce, quod sciens Christus quid esset id se quod non erat exhiberet? Non potes dicere, Ne si natus fuisset et hominem induisset, deus esse desisset, amittens quod erat, dum fit quod non erat. Periculum enim status sui deo nullum est. Sed ideo, inquis, nego deum in hominem vere conversum, ita ut et nasceretur et carne corporaretur, quia qui sine fine est etiam inconvertibilis sit necesse est. Converti enim in aliud finis est pristini. Non competit ergo conversio cui non competit finis. Plane natura convertibilium ea lege est, ne permaneant in eo quod convertitur in eis, et ita non permanendo pereant, dum perdunt convertendo quod fuerunt. Sed nihil deo par est; natura eius ab omnium rerum condicione distat Si ergo quae a deo distant, a quibus deus distat, cum convertuntur amittunt quod fuerunt, ubi erit diversitas divinitatis a ceteris rebus, nisi ut contrarium obtineat, id est ut deus et in omnia converti possit et qualis est perseverare? Aliequin par erit eorum quae conversa amittunt quod fuerunt, quorum utique in omnibus par non est, sic nec in exitu conversionis. Angelos creatoris conversos in effigiem humanam aliquando legisti, et credidisti, et tantam corporis gestasse veritatem, ut et pedes eis laverit Abraham, et manibus ipsorum ereptus sit Sodomitis Loth, conluctatus quoque homini angelus toto corporis pondere dimitti desideraverit, adeo detinebatur. Quod enim angelis inferioribus dei licuit conversis in corpulentiam humanam, ut angeli nihilominus permanerent, hoc tu potentiori deo auferes, qussi non valuerit Christus vere hominem indutus deus perseverare? Aut numquid et angeli illi phantasmata carnis apparuerunt? Sed non audebis hoc dicere. Nam si sic apud te angeli creatoris sicut et Christus, eius dei erit Christus cuius angeli tales qualis et Christus. Si scripturas opinioni tuae resistentes non de industria alias reiecisses, alias corrupisses, confudisset te in hac specie evangelium Ioannis, praedicans spiritum columbae corpore lapsum desedisse super dominum. Qui spiritus cum hoc esset, tam vere erat et columba quam et spiritus, nec interfecerat substantiam propriam assumpta substantia extranea. Sed quaeris corpus columbae ubi sit resumpto spiritu in caelum, aeque et angelorum. Eadem ratione interceptum est qua et editum fuerat. Si vidisses cum de nihilo proferebatur, scisses et cum in nihilum subducebatur. Si non fuit initium visihile, nec finis. Tamen corporis soliditas erat, quoquo momento corpus videbatur. Non potest non fuisse quod scriptum est.
thought_title: God's will and power to be born without change
orientation: Tertullian is answering Marcion's objection that birth was impossible or unworthy for God, arguing that God could be born and remain God.
pass_a_gloss: It is necessary, insofar as you think this was permitted to your judgment, that you have considered the birth either impossible or unfitting for God. But nothing is impossible for God except what he does not will. Therefore let us consider whether he willed to be born (because if he willed, he both could and was born). I run to a short cut. For if God had not willed to be born, for whatever cause, he would not have presented himself to be seen as a man. For who, seeing him as a man, would deny that he was born? Thus what he had not willed to be, he would not have willed to be seen at all. The opinion of every displeasing thing is also rejected, because it makes no difference whether a thing is or is not, if when it is not it is presumed to be. Clearly it matters that what truly is not should not suffer a falsehood. But his own conscience was enough for him, you say. Let men see if they thought he was born, because they saw him as a man. How much more worthy therefore and how much more consistent would he have sustained human estimation truly born, being about to undergo the same estimation even not born with injury to his own conscience, which you reckon as confidence, so that not born he would sustain against his own conscience being thought born? What was of such great value, teach, that Christ knowing what he was should exhibit himself as what he was not? You cannot say, Lest if he had been born and had put on man, he would have ceased to be God, losing what he was, while he becomes what he was not. For there is no danger to God of his own state. But for this reason, you say, I deny that God was truly turned into man, so that he both was born and was embodied in flesh, because he who is without end must also be unchangeable. For to be turned into another thing is the end of the former. Therefore conversion does not suit him to whom end does not suit. Clearly the nature of changeable things is under this law, that they do not remain in that into which they are turned, and so by not remaining they perish, while by being turned they lose what they were. But nothing is equal to God; his nature differs from the condition of all things. If therefore those things which differ from God, from which God differs, when they are turned lose what they were, where will be the difference of divinity from other things, unless it obtains the contrary, that is that God both can be turned into all things and persevere as he is? Otherwise he will be equal to those things which when turned lose what they were, to which certainly he is not equal in all things, so neither in the outcome of conversion. You have read at some time the angels of the creator turned into human appearance, and you believed, and that they carried such truth of body, that Abraham washed their feet, and Lot was rescued from the Sodomites by their hands, and an angel wrestling with a man desired to be released with the whole weight of his body, so much was he held. For what was permitted to the lower angels of God, turned into human corpulence, that they nevertheless remained angels, this you will take away from the more powerful God, as if Christ truly clothed with man had not been able to persevere God? Or were those angels also phantoms of flesh? But you will not dare to say this. For if the angels of the creator are with you as also Christ, Christ will be of that God whose angels are such as also Christ. If you had not deliberately rejected some scriptures resisting your opinion, and corrupted others, the Gospel of John would have confounded you in this appearance, preaching that the spirit in the body of a dove glided down and settled upon the Lord. Which spirit when it was this, was as truly a dove as also spirit, nor had it destroyed its own substance by assuming an extraneous substance. But you ask where the body of the dove is when the spirit was taken back into heaven, and equally of the angels. By the same reason it was taken away as it had been brought forth. If you had seen when it was brought forth from nothing, you would know also when it was withdrawn into nothing. If the beginning was not visible, neither was the end. Nevertheless the solidity of the body was, at whatever moment the body was seen. What is written cannot not have been.

choices.why: Glossary requires 'birth' for nativitas, especially Christ's true birth from the Virgin Mary.
Glossary requires 'phantom' for phantasma, the heretical view of Christ's body as unreal appearance.
Keeps the physical, bodily weight and solidity Tertullian emphasizes, contrasting with phantom.
Glossary requires 'substance' for substantia, the underlying reality of a thing.
Renders the negative adjective literally, matching Tertullian's argument that God cannot be turned into another thing.
Keeps the root sense of 'turning into' that Tertullian plays on throughout the passage.

bible_refs.note: Abraham washed the feet of the angels who appeared as men.

pass_b_english: It follows necessarily, since you think you had the right to decide this, that you judged birth either impossible for God or unworthy of him. But nothing is impossible for God except what he does not will. Let us consider, then, whether he willed the birth—because if he willed it, he both could do it and was born. I take the short way. If God had not willed the birth, for whatever reason, he would not have presented himself as a man to be seen. For who, seeing him as a man, would deny that he had been born? So what he had not willed to be, he would not have willed to be seen at all. The mere opinion of anything displeasing is rejected, because it makes no difference whether a thing exists or not, if when it does not exist it is presumed to exist. Of course it matters that what truly does not exist should not suffer a false report. But, you say, his own conscience was enough for him. Let people think he was born if they wanted, since they saw a man. How much more worthy, then, and how much more consistent it would have been for him to have endured human opinion as one truly born, rather than to undergo that same opinion without the birth, to the injury of his own conscience—which you count as confidence—so that, not born, he would endure being thought born against his own conscience? Tell me what was worth so much that Christ, knowing what he was, should present himself as what he was not. You cannot say, "If he had been born and put on man, he would have ceased to be God, losing what he was while becoming what he was not." For there is no danger to God's own state. But, you say, I deny that God was truly turned into man, so as to undergo birth and be embodied in flesh, because one who is without end must also be unchangeable. For to be turned into another thing is the end of the former thing. Conversion therefore does not suit one whom end does not suit. Clearly, the nature of changeable things has this law: they do not remain in what they are turned into, and so by not remaining they perish, losing what they were by being converted. But nothing is equal to God; his nature stands apart from the condition of all things. If, then, the things that stand apart from God—from which God stands apart—lose what they were when they are converted, where will the difference of divinity from other things be, unless it holds the opposite, that is, that God can be turned into all things and still persevere as he is? Otherwise he will be equal to those things which, when converted, lose what they were—and since he is not equal to them in all things, neither is he in the outcome of conversion. You have read at some time that the Creator's angels were turned into human appearance, and you believed it, and that they carried such truth of body that Abraham washed their feet (Genesis 18:4), and Lot was rescued from the Sodomites by their hands (Genesis 19:16), and an angel also wrestled with a man and desired to be released with the whole weight of his body, so firmly was he held (Genesis 32:24-26). What was permitted to the lower angels of God—to be converted into human bodily form and yet remain angels—will you take away from the more powerful God, as if Christ, truly clothed in man, could not have persevered as God? Or did those angels also appear as phantoms of flesh? But you will not dare to say this. For if in your view the Creator's angels are as Christ is, then Christ will belong to that God whose angels are such as Christ is. If you had not deliberately rejected some Scriptures that resist your opinion and corrupted others, the Gospel of John would have confounded you on this point, preaching that the Spirit in bodily form of a dove descended and settled upon the Lord (John 1:32). That Spirit, since it was this, was as truly a dove as it was the Spirit, and it had not destroyed its own substance by taking on an external substance. But you ask where the body of the dove is, once the Spirit was taken back into heaven—and likewise the bodies of the angels. It was withdrawn by the same means by which it had been produced. If you had seen it when it was brought forth from nothing, you would know also when it was withdrawn into nothing. If its beginning was not visible, neither was its end. Yet the body had solidity, at whatever moment the body was seen. What is written cannot not have been.

problems.why: Tertullian means 'bodily substance/physical body,' not obesity; 'corpulence' means fatness in modern English.
problems.ruling: Latin "in corpulentiam humanam" means ‘into human flesh/body’; translating as “human corpulence” suggests obesity, altering theological sense.

fixed: Changed 'corpulence' to 'bodily form': source 'corpulentiam' means bodily substance/physical body, not fatness.

last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'auferes' is rhetorical question (cf. preceding 'Quid tanti fuit'); future indicative regularly functions thus. Meaning unchanged.
